1 · ATMOSPHERE#

  • Layer of air surrounding the Earth.
  • Importance:
    • It protects the earth from the harmful radiation from the sun. The Ozone Layer absorbs harmful UV radiations.
    • The Greenhouse Effect by certains gases in the atmosphere helps keep the Earth warm, to allow the survival of life.
    • The atmosphere also takes care of extra-terrestrial objects like meteors that get burnt up while passing through it, due to air friction.
  • The gasses of the present atmosphere are a product of volcanic eruptions , hot springs, chemical breakdowns of solid matter, and redistribution from the biosphere.
  • Composition of the atmosphere:
    • The atmosphere is a mixture of many gases. In addition, it contains huge numbers of solid and liquid particles, collectively called aerosols.
    • Nitrogen and oxygen make up nearly 99% of the clean, dry air . The remaining gases are mostly inert and constitute about 1% of the atmosphere.
    • Oxygen constitutes 21% of the total volume of the atmosphere. All living organisms inhale oxygen . Besides, oxygen can combine with other elements to form important compounds, such as oxides. Also, combustion is not possible without oxygen.
    • Nitrogen accounts for 78% of total atmospheric volume. It is a relatively inert gas and is an important constituent of all organic compounds. The main function of nitrogen is to control combustion by diluting oxygen .
    • Carbon Dioxide: constitutes only about 0.038% (now 0.04%) of the dry air and is a product of combustion. Green plants, through photosynthesis, absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and use it to manufacture food and keep other biophysical processes going. It is an important greenhouse gas, and helps maintain the Heat Budget of Earth.
    • Carbon dioxide and water vapour are found only up to 90 km from the surface of the

earth.

    • Water vapour depends on temperature and therefore it decreases from the equator poleward in response to changes in temperature (and evaporation).
      • 0 to 5 % by volume; More than 90% found up to the height of 5 km.
    • Argon: The third important gas which constitutes only about 0.93%.
    • Ozone (O3)
      • Formed at higher altitudes and transported downwards .
      • The ozone layer is between 20 km and 25 km altitude where the greatest concentrations of ozone are found.
      • Protects from harmful UV radiations.
    • Other gases: Neon, helium, hydrogen, xenon, krypton, methane.
PDF p.112
    • Particulate Matter: Consists of sand particles (from weathered rocks, and volcanic ash), pollen grains, small organisms, soot, and ocean salts ; the upper layers of the atmosphere may even have fragments of meteors .
      • Help in the absorbing, reflecting, and scattering of the solar radiation which adds the varied charming colours of red and orange at sunrise and sunset.
      • Salt particles become hygroscopic nuclei and thus help in the formation of water drops , clouds, and various forms of condensation and precipitation.
      • Recent research: Microplastics in the atmosphere can act as nuclei for cloud formation, leading to ice crystal formation at temperatures 5 to 10 degrees Celsius warmer than usual.

Layers Of The Atmosphere:

  • Based on Composition:
    • Homosphere : Up to 80 km . The gases are distributed uniformly , therefore, there is a homogenous composition.
    • Heterosphere: Beyond 80 km . Here the gases are layered according to their molecular masses.
  • Based on Change in the temperature:
    • Troposphere: 8-18 km (13 km avg.)
      • It is thicker at the equator (18 km) due to the strong convection experienced here. It's thinner at the poles (8 km).
      • Temperature change: Temperature gradually decreases with height,

approx. 1℃ for every 165 meters

(normal lapse rate).

      • Why does the temperature reduce? The prime source of heat for the troposphere is terrestrial radiation. As the distance from the surface of the earth increases , the temperature reduces.
      • All weather phenomena like cloud

formation, movement of air masses and jet streams, etc , take place in this layer.

      • It is separated from the stratosphere by Tropopause.
    • Stratosphere: Upto 50 kilometres above the earth's surface, beyond the tropopause.
      • Ozone layer : Present in the lower part of the stratosphere . The absorption of ultraviolet (UV) energy from the sun by this ozone causes the temperature to rise with height.
      • Temperatures are highest over the summer pole and lowest over the winter pole in the stratosphere.
      • This layer is almost free from clouds and associated weather phenomena, making conditions most ideal for flying

aeroplanes.

      • Sometimes, rarely, cirrus clouds are present at lower levels in this layer.
    • Mesosphere: 50-80 km.
      • Up to the Mesopause
      • The coldest layer of the atmosphere, where the temperature again reduces with the height.
      • The air is so cold just below the mesopause that even the scarce water vapour can be sublimated into polar-mesospheric noctilucent clouds .
PDF p.113
      • Most of the meteors burn up in this layer.
    • Thermosphere: 80-400 km.
      • Above the mesopause, temperatures again increase with height. Due to the absorption of energetic ultraviolet and X-ray radiation from the sun.
      • The International Space Station and satellites orbit here.
      • The Kármán line , located at an altitude of 100 km : is widely used to describe the border between Earth's atmosphere and outer space .
      • Ionosphere is a part of this layer, where electrically charged currents flow in the air in this sphere. Radio waves are reflected on the earth from this sphere and due to this radio broadcasting has become possible.
    • Exosphere: Beyond 400 km; High temperature of air particles , but less density , so temperature reduces with height .
      • Above the ionosphere and extends to 400 km above the earth.
      • The air here is extremely rareﬁed .
      • Due to proximity to solar radiations, the temperature of air particles can go up to

1000 ℃.

      • But due to low density, the air particles are so far apart that they are unable to transfer the temperature.
      • Thus, the temperature feels cold.

Heat & Temperature

  • The interaction of insolation with the atmosphere and the earth’s surface creates heat , which is measured in terms of temperature.
  • The distribution of temperature varies both horizontally and vertically.
  • Factors affecting the distribution of temperature:
    • The latitude, which determines the angle of inclination. The higher the angle of inclination, more the distance sun rays have to travel within the atmosphere, which increases the heat lost by the sun rays. So, less heat is transferred to the Earth. This is why the poles, which get slanting solar radiation, are much cooler than the equator, which gets direct sunlight.
    • Duration of sunlight: During the summers, the duration of sunlight is more than during the winters (except at the equator, where day and night are equal). So, summers are warmer.
    • Sunspot Cycle (discussed in the Universe part)
    • Transparency of the atmosphere : On a cloudy day, the clouds obstruct the sunlight from reaching the earth’s surface, which is why cloudy days are cooler. On the other hand, cloudy nights are warmer as the clouds do not allow terrestrial radiation to escape. The same happens when there are lots of aerosols and particulate matter in the atmosphere.
    • Altitude of the place: as the altitude increases, the temperature reduces per the Normal Lapse rate.
    • Orientation: The places to the North of mountain ranges in the Northern Hemisphere, north of the Tropic of Cancer, and those to the South of the Mountain Ranges, south of the Tropic of Capricorn, are perpetually in the shadow of the mountains (until the mountains are eroded).
    • Vegetation cover: Trees undertake transpiration, which has a cooling effect on the environment.
    • Distance from the sea: The continental locations have more extreme temperatures than the coastal locations, due to the moderating impact of the ocean/sea through the land and sea breezes.
    • Ocean Currents: Warm and cold ocean currents increase or reduce the temperature of the place respectively.
    • Local factors like local winds, urban area distribution, etc , can also affect the temperature of a location.

Ways of heat transfer:

  • Conduction: Transfer of heat through a solid material from molecule to molecule .
PDF p.114
    • Mechanism: Direct contact between particles , with heat moving from a region of higher temperature to one of lower temperature.
    • Example: A metal rod heated at one end will gradually transfer heat to the other end.
  • Convection: Transfer of heat by the movement of a fluid (liquid or gas).
    • Mechanism: Warmer, less dense fluid rises while cooler, denser fluid sinks , creating a circulation pattern.
    • Example: Boiling water, where hot water rises to the surface and cooler water sinks to the bottom.
  • Advection: Transfer of heat through the horizontal movement of air or water .
    • Mechanism: Large-scale horizontal movement of fluid carrying heat from one place to another.
    • Example: Warm air moving into a region from another area, such as warm winds bringing heat to a cooler area.
  • Radiation: Transfer of heat through electromagnetic waves without the need for a medium .
    • Mechanism: Heat is emitted as

infrared radiation and can travel through a vacuum .

    • Example: The heat from the sun warming the Earth. Horizontal temperature distribution:
    • Distribution of temperature across the latitudes over the surface of the earth.
    • Shown by “Isotherms”
    • Generally, from the equator to poleward , the temperature keeps on declining .
    • In general, the equatorial region is hot , and its temperature is high throughout the year.
    • The lowest temperature is at and near the poles.
    • The amount of insolation received varies from latitude to latitude.
    • Regions within the equator and 40° N and S latitudes receive abundant sunlight and hence more heat will be gained than lost. Hence, they are energy surplus regions.
    • Regions beyond 40° N and S latitudes lose more heat than that gained from sunlight. Hence, they are energy deﬁcit regions.
    • The atmosphere (planetary winds) and the oceans (ocean currents) transfer excess heat from the tropics (energy surplus region) towards the poles (energy deﬁcit regions)
    • Most of the heat transfer takes place across the mid-latitudes (30° to 50°), hence the high frequency of storms here.
  • Heat Budget: The earth receives a certain amount of Insolation (incoming short-wave solar radiation) and gives back heat into space by terrestrial radiation (outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation). Through this give and take, or the heat budget, the earth maintains a constant temperature.
PDF p.115

Albedo

  • Albedo is a measure of the reflectivity of a surface , indicating how much solar radiation is reflected by that surface compared to how much is absorbed.
  • Surfaces with high albedo , such as snow and ice , reflect a large portion of incoming solar radiation, contributing to cooling.
  • Conversely, dark surfaces like oceans, forests, and urban areas have low albedo and absorb more solar radiation, leading to warming.
  • Short and Long wave radiation: The higher the temperature of the body, the shorter the wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation released by it. Since the sun has a higher temperature than the Earth, the EMRs from the sun to the Earth are called Short wave radiations, and the EMRs released by the Earth are called Long wave radiations.
  • Vertical Distribution of Temperature: Covered under “Layers of Atmosphere”.= ISOTHERMS
  • Isotherms are the lines joining locations with same temperature.
    • Bending of isotherms refers to the way lines of equal temperature (isotherms) on weather maps deviate from their expected straight east-west pattern.
    • This occurs due to factors like:
PDF p.116
      • Land-sea contrast: Land heats and cools faster than water, causing isotherms to bend inland in summer and towards the coast in winter .
  • In Northern Hemisphere (NH):
    • In July, isotherms shift towards equator on land, and towards pole on oceans. In January the isotherms deviate to the pole over the ocean and to the equator over the continent.
  • In Southern Hemisphere (SH), this shift is not very evident due to lack of land. But, though at smaller scale, due to opposite seasons in this hemisphere compared to NH, the shift here is opposite. What NH sees in January, is seen here in July, and vice versa.
  • To summarize, in July, isotherms shift to south over oceans, and north over land. In January the isotherms deviate to the north over the ocean and to the south over the continent.
      • Ocean currents: Warm or cold currents can cause isotherms to bulge or curve depending on their temperature.
      • Topography: Mountains can block or channel air masses , leading to localized temperature variations and bending of isotherms.

2 · PYQ#

Q.1) A layer in the Earth’s atmosphere called Ionosphere facilitates radio communication. Why? 1. The presence of ozone causes the reflection of radio waves to Earth. 2. Radio waves have a very long wavelength. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (2011) (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2

Answer: D The ionosphere is deﬁned as the layer of the Earth's atmosphere that is ionized by solar and cosmic radiation.

  • It lies 75-1000 km (46-621 miles) above the Earth.
  • (The Earth’s radius is 6370 km, so the thickness of the ionosphere is quite tiny compared with the size of Earth.)
  • Because of the high energy from the Sun and from cosmic rays, the atoms in this area have been stripped of one or more of their electrons, or “ionized,” and are therefore positively charged. The ionized electrons behave as free particles.
  • The Sun's upper atmosphere, the corona, is very hot and produces a constant stream of plasma and UV and X-rays that flow out from the Sun and affect or ionize the Earth's ionosphere.
  • Only half the Earth’s ionosphere is being ionized by the Sun at any time.
  • The ionosphere has major importance to us because, among other functions, it influences radio propagation to distant places on the Earth, and between satellites and Earth.
  • For the very low frequency (VLF) waves that the space weather monitors track, the ionosphere and the ground produce a “waveguide” through which radio signals can bounce and make their way around the curved Earth
  • The ionosphere is composed of three main parts, named for obscure historical reasons: the D, E, and F regions.
  • The electron density is highest in the upper, or F region.
  • The F region exists during both daytime and nighttime.
  • During the day it is ionized by solar radiation, during the night by cosmic rays.
  • The D region disappears during the night compared to the daytime, and the E region becomes weakened.
PDF p.117
  • Wavelength of radio waves can be 1 milimeter to 100 km, so they are not “very long wavelength waves.

Q.2) Normally, the temperature decreases with the increase in height from the Earth’s surface, because 1. the atmosphere can be heated upwards only from the Earth’s surface 2. there is more moisture in the upper atmosphere 3. the air is less dense in the upper atmosphere Select the correct answer using the codes given below : (2012) (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3

Answer: C The ﬁrst statement given in this question is correct.

  • Temperature falls off with height at a predictable rate because the air near the surface is heated and becomes light, and the air higher up cools to space and becomes heavy.
  • The second statement is obviously incorrect. This is because the water vapour, which accounts for around 1% of air, varies greatly in the troposphere and decreases rapidly with altitude.
  • As we increase elevation, there is less air above us thus the pressure decreases. As the pressure decreases, air molecules spread out further (i.e. air expands), and the temperature decreases and the atmosphere can be heated upwards only from the Earth's surface.
  • Near the Earth's surface, air gets cooler the higher you climb. As you climb a mountain, you can expect the air temperature to decrease by 6.5 degrees C for every 1000 meters you gain. This is called the standard (average) lapse rate.
  • The basic answer is that the farther away you get from the earth, the thinner the atmosphere gets. The total heat content of a system is directly related to the amount of matter present, so it is cooler at higher elevations

Q.3) The increasing amount of carbon dioxide in the air is slowly raising the temperature of the atmosphere because it absorbs - (2012) (a) the water vapour of the air and retains its heat (b) the ultraviolet part of the solar radiation (c) all the solar radiations (d) Infrared part of solar radiation

Answer: D Carbon dioxide is meteorologically a very important gas as it is transparent to the incoming solar radiation but opaque to the outgoing terrestrial radiation.

  • It absorbs a part of terrestrial radiation and reflects back some part of it towards the earth’s surface. It is largely responsible for the greenhouse effect.
  • Its concentration is greater close to the earth’s surface as it is denser than air.

Q.4) The annual range of temperature in the interior of the continents is high as compared to coastal areas. What is/are the reason/reasons? (2013) 1. Thermal difference between land and water 2. Variation in altitude between continents and oceans 3. Presence of strong winds in the interior 4. Heavy rains in the interior as compared to coasts Select the correct answer using the codes given below. (a) 1 only (b) 1 and 2 only (c) 2 and 3 only

PDF p.118

(d) 1, 2, 3 and 4

Answer: A

  • The major factor affecting the distribution of the temperature of Earth is distribution of Land and Oceans. Since there is more land in the Northern Hemisphere and more waters in the Southern hemisphere, there is a big difference between the speciﬁc heat of land and water; the loss of heat from the continents is bigger than the oceans. The continents get heated faster and get cooled faster in comparison to the Oceans. This is the reason that the temperatures of the Oceans are moderate while that of continents is extreme. The moderating effect on temperature of the land due to proximity of the seas is called Maritime influence. The increasing effect on temperature of the land at the interior of the continents is called Continental Influence.
  • Due to this moderating effect of the sea , places near the coast have a low range of temperature and high humidity.The places in the interior of the continent do not experience the moderating effects of the sea. These places have extreme temperatures.
  • Statement 4 claims that Heavy rains in the interior as compared to coasts (are responsible for why the annual range of temperature in the interior of the continent is high)
  • But the interiors in Central Asia receive very poor rainfall due to the distance from the sea. Annual precipitation is usually low in the interior areas. Hence 4 cannot be the answer

Statement-II: The speciﬁc heat of water is more than that of land surface. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? Answer: D

  • Water has a very high speciﬁc heat, which means that in order to increase or reduce its temperature by 1 degree celsius, it will have to absorb or release huge amount of heat. Compare t that, the land has low speciﬁc heat, and can heat up or cool down fast.

Q.10) Consider the following statements: Statement I: In January, in the Northern Hemisphere, the isotherms bend equatorward while crossing the landmasses, and poleward while crossing the oceans. Statement II: In January, the air over the oceans is warmer than that over the landmasses in the Northern Hemisphere. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? (2025) (a) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I (b) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II does not explain Statement I (c) Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct (d) Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct

Answer: (a) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I Statement I: Correct

  • In January (winter in the Northern Hemisphere), isotherms (lines of equal temperature) bend equatorward over landmasses because land cools faster than water.
PDF p.120
  • Over oceans, where temperatures remain relatively warm, isotherms bend poleward.
  • This distortion of isotherms is a well-known climatological feature seen on global isotherm maps for January. Statement II: Correct
  • Due to higher speciﬁc heat and slower cooling, oceans retain more heat than land during winter. Hence, in January, air over oceans is warmer than over land.
  • This temperature differential explains why maritime climates are milder than continental ones in winter.

3 · Temperature Inversion:#

  • Inversion of the normal lapse rate , such that as the altitude increases, the temperature starts to increase too.
  • Conditions for Temperature Inversion:
    • Clear, Calm Conditions: Clear skies and calm winds allow for efﬁcient radiative cooling of the Earth's surface during the night.
    • Long Nights or Extended Darkness: Longer nights or periods of extended darkness allow for more signiﬁcant radiative cooling of the surface air.
    • Absence of Atmospheric Mixing: A lack of vertical mixing, such as from strong winds or convective activity, prevents the mixing of warmer air aloft with cooler air near the surface, allowing the inversion layer to form and persist.
    • Geographic Features : Certain geographic features, such as valleys or basins, can enhance the likelihood of temperature inversion by trapping cold air near the surface, especially during calm, clear nights.
  • Most commonly seen at:
    • Fronts
    • Winter season
    • Mountains & Valleys

Positive and Negative Impacts

Positive:

  • Frost Protection for Plants: The warmer air above the inversion layer can prevent ground temperatures from dropping too low, protecting crops from frost damage. Negative:
  • Pollution Dome Effect
  • Reduced Visibility due to fog formation, affects transportation.
  • Can create conditions where pests and diseases thrive , potentially harming crops if not managed properly. Pollution Dome Effect:
  • The pollution dome effect refers to the phenomenon where pollutants become trapped beneath a layer of warm air during temperature inversion events.
  • During a temperature inversion, a layer of warm air traps cooler air beneath it, along with any pollutants present in the lower atmosphere. This creates a "dome" or "cap" of stagnant air that prevents the vertical dispersion of pollutants.
  • This usually happens during cold weather, when the air in contact with the cold ground becomes cool, resulting in temperature inversion.
  • Temperature Inversion's Role: Temperature inversion exacerbates the pollution dome effect by preventing vertical mixing of the atmosphere . Normally, warmer air rises and cooler air sinks, facilitating the dispersal of pollutants. However, during inversion, this
PDF p.122

vertical movement is suppressed, leading to the accumulation of pollutants near the surface.

  • Consequences: The pollution dome effect can lead to increased concentrations of pollutants in affected areas , resulting in poor air quality and health hazards for residents. In severe cases, prolonged exposure to high levels of pollutants trapped within the dome can lead to respiratory problems, cardiovascular issues, and other health complications .
  • Mitigation : Strategies to mitigate the pollution dome effect include reducing emissions of pollutants at their sources, implementing air quality monitoring and forecasting systems , and promoting public awareness and behaviour change to reduce individual contributions to air pollution.
  • In 2013, China launched a $100-billion initiative to combat air pollution in Beijing, implementing strict regulations on vehicle emissions, relocating polluting industries, and promoting cleaner energy sources. As a result, Beijing's air quality improved substantially, with PM2.5 levels decreasing by 35% between 2013 and 2017.

4 · AIR PRESSURE & PRESSURE BELTS#

  • Total weight of a mass of column of air above per unit area at sea level.
  • Maximum at sea level
  • High-temperature results in Low

Pressure and vice versa.

  • When the air gets heated it expands, becomes light and rises vertically. As air rises, the pressure it exerts on the Earth’s surface is reduced, causing a low-pressure area. On the other hand, cool air is dense and heavy. As a result, it sinks vertically. It results in additional weight and pressure which causes a high pressure on the ground.
  • Lines joining places with equal

pressure are called Isobars.

  • Based on temperature distribution, 7 pressure belts are present on the Earth.
    • 3 of these are thermally induced , created due to the temperature.
    • 4 are dynamically induced due to the movement of the winds from the thermally induced pressure belts.
  • The Equatorial Low-Pressure belt (10 degrees north and south) is also known as the ITCZ (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone) or the “Doldrums” (calms), as this region experiences monotonous windless weather , due to the convergence of the trade winds around it.
  • Pressure belts are not homogenous , due to uneven distribution of land and water.
  • Pressure belts shift due to the revolution of Earth because of Earth’s 23.5-degree tilt , depending upon where the sunlight falls directly.
  • In the Northern Hemisphere, January denotes winter, and July denotes summer. In the Southern Hemisphere, the opposite is true. The pressure belts shift approx 5°- 10° northward (can be as high as 25° over India) when the sun shines vertically overhead on the Tropic of Cancer (21 June), and approx 5°- 10° southward when the sun shines vertically overhead on the Tropic of Capricorn (22 December) from their initial position.
  • Seasonal climate fluctuations are caused by the movement of the pressure belts , especially between the latitudes of 30° and 40° (Mediterranean Climate) in both hemispheres. During winter, Westerlies prevail, resulting in rain. During the summer, dry Trade Winds blow offshore, preventing rain from falling in certain areas.
  • The pressure belts in both hemispheres stay balanced when the sun shines vertically over the Equator on March 21st and September 23rd (the Equinoxes).
PDF p.123

WINDS: FACTORS AFFECTING THEIR MOVEMENT

  • Pressure Gradient (Direction and Speed) : It denotes the pressure difference between two locations. The winds always move from the High to the Low-pressure region. This determines the direction of the winds.
    • The steep Pressure Gradient is denoted on the maps via closely spaced isobars. The steeper the gradient is, the higher the speed of movement of the winds.
    • So overall, this force determines both the speed and the direction of the wind movement i.e. it helps determine the overall velocity of the Winds.
  • Coriolis Force (Only Direction)
    • This force is generated by virtue of the movement of the Earth and affects only the objects or entities moving on the surface of the Earth , like winds and ocean currents. That is why it is an apparent and not a real force.
    • It affects only the direction of movement of the winds.
    • The magnitude of deflection depends upon the speed of the wind . Higher speed means higher deflection.
    • Deflects the winds to the Right in the Northern Hemisphere.
    • Deflects the winds to the Left in the Southern Hemisphere.
    • 0 at the equator, maximum at the poles.
  • Frictional Force (Direction and Speed):
    • It is the force experienced by the winds in the direction opposite to its movement.
    • It can affect both the direction and the speed of wind movement.
    • It is effective only up to a few thousand meters above the Earth’s surface.
    • The oceans provide much less frictional force than land, as the latter is covered with vegetation, infrastructure, landforms, etc. That is why the wind speeds are higher over water bodies than on the land.

TYPES OF WINDS

  • Prevailing/Primary/Planetary/Permanent winds: These winds get affected by all the abovementioned forces and affect the Earth’s surface throughout the year. E.g. Trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies.
  • Geostrophic Winds: They move at tropopause-ic level, and therefore are not affected by the frictional force . As a result, they travel parallel to the isobars. E.g. Jet streams.
  • Seasonal Winds: They are experienced only during a particular season. E.g. Monsoonal winds.
  • Diurnal winds: change direction between day and night. E.g. in coastal regions, the sea breeze blows during the day and the land breeze blows during the night. Another example is the mountain valley breeze.
  • Local Winds: Winds that affect only a speciﬁc location. May be all year round, or during a particular season.

NOMENCLATURE OF WINDS

  • Winds are named after the direction from which they seem to be coming . E.g. Polar easterlies are named so as they come from the eastern direction. They have an east-to-west movement.

PLANETARY WINDS AND TRI-CELLULAR MERIDIONAL CIRCULATION:

  • Planetary winds are large-scale wind patterns that circulate the Earth , driven by differences in temperature and pressure between regions.
  • They are present throughout the Year .
  • These winds play a crucial role in redistributing heat and moisture across the planet , influencing weather patterns and climate. There are several key types of planetary winds:
    • Trade Winds : Trade winds are

persistent easterly winds that blow

PDF p.124

from the subtropical high-pressure belts towards the equator in both hemispheres. They are named "trade winds" because they historically facilitated trade routes across the world's oceans. Trade winds play a signiﬁcant role in the movement of ocean currents and are important for sailors and aviation routes.

    • Westerlies : Westerlies are prevailing winds that blow from the subtropical high-pressure belts towards the sub-polar low-pressure region in both

hemispheres. They are characterized by their westerly direction (from west to east) and play a crucial role in the movement of weather systems across mid-latitudes. The westerlies are particularly strong and well-deﬁned in the Southern Hemisphere and flow at extremely high speeds. This has given them the names like roaring fourties, furious ﬁfties, and shrieking sixties.

    • Polar Easterlies : Polar easterlies are cold winds that blow from the polar high-pressure belts towards the mid-latitudes in both hemispheres . They are characterized by their easterly direction (from east to west) and are influenced by the temperature gradient between the polar regions and the mid-latitudes. Polar easterlies are weaker and less consistent than the trade winds and westerlies.
  • Tricellular Meridional Circulation: Tricellular meridional circulation refers to the three-cell circulation pattern in each hemisphere of the Earth's atmosphere, characterized by the movement of air from the equator towards the poles and back again.
    • Hadley Cell : The Hadley cell is the largest and most prominent cell in the tricellular circulation, extending from the equator to about 30 degrees latitude . Warm, moist air rises at the equator, forming low-pressure zones and generating trade winds. As the air cools and descends around 30 degrees latitude, it creates high-pressure belts and generates the trade winds.
    • Ferrel Cell : The Ferrel cell is a mid-latitude cell that lies between the Hadley and polar cells. It operates in the opposite direction to the Hadley cell, with air rising at around 60 degrees latitude and descending at around 30 degrees latitude. The Ferrel cell is driven by the interaction between the Hadley and polar cells.
    • Polar Cell : The polar cell is the smallest and weakest in the tricellular circulation, extending from around 60 degrees latitude to the poles. Cold, dense air sinks at the poles, creating high-pressure zones and generating the polar easterlies. As the air warms and rises around 60 degrees latitude, it creates low-pressure belts and generates westerly winds.
    • Importance : Tricellular meridional circulation plays a crucial role in regulating global climate and weather patterns by transporting heat, moisture, and energy around the planet. It helps to redistribute heat from the equator towards the poles and vice versa, influencing temperature gradients, atmospheric pressure systems, and wind patterns.

6 · GEOSTROPHIC WINDS:#

  • Geostrophic winds are large-scale winds that blow parallel to isobars (lines of constant pressure) in the atmosphere. They are the result of a balance between the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force , acting perpendicular to the pressure gradient.
  • Formation : Geostrophic winds form when the pressure gradient force , which drives air from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure, is balanced by the Coriolis force , which deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and the left in the Southern Hemisphere due to the Earth's rotation.

7 · JET STREAMS#

  • Jet streams are narrow bands of fast-flowing, high-altitude winds found in the upper atmosphere, typically at altitudes of 8 to 15 kilometres. They are characterized by their high wind speeds and meandering, ribbon-like appearance.
  • Formation : Jet streams are primarily formed by the interaction between the temperature gradients of different air masses. The largest and most well-known jet streams are the polar jet stream and the subtropical jet stream, which are located near the boundaries of the polar and tropical air masses, respectively.
  • Wavy Jet Streams are said to have “ Rossby Wave ” characteristics.
    • Coriolis force and reduction in temperature contrast, can lead to the Rossby wave characteristic. Due to climate change, the Jet streams are weakening and becoming more meandering.
  • Types : They can be permanent or seasonal.
    • Permanent: Polar Jet Streams, Sub-tropical Jet streams
    • Temporary : Tropical Easterly Jet, Somali Jet Stream.
  • Polar Jet Stream : The polar jet stream is located at high latitudes, typically between 50 and 60 degrees north and south of the equator. It forms along the boundary between cold polar air to the north and warmer subtropical air to the south. The polar jet stream is strongest in winter and weaker in summer , and it plays a crucial role in steering weather systems and influencing storm tracks.
  • Subtropical Jet Stream : The subtropical jet stream is located at lower latitudes , typically between 20 and 30 degrees north and south of the equator . It forms along the boundary between warm tropical air to the south and cooler mid-latitude air to the north. The subtropical jet stream is weaker and less consistent than the polar jet stream but still influences weather patterns and atmospheric circulation.
  • Impact on Weather & Economy :
    • Jet streams play a signiﬁcant role in shaping weather patterns by steering the movement of weather systems and influencing the development of storms and precipitation.
    • They move air masses from one place to another, leading to the development of fronts and extratropical cyclones.
    • They can also affect aviation routes , with aircraft often taking advantage of the strong tailwinds associated with jet streams to reduce flight times and fuel consumption.
    • Jet Stream may transport ozone-depleting substances higher up in the stratosphere. This vertical air circulation causes a rapid rate of mixing of air between the Troposphere & Stratosphere.
    • The Monsoon of South Asia is largely controlled & affected by Jet Streams.
    • In India, they bring Western disturbances which are extra-tropical cyclones of the Mediterranean, dragged into India by the subtropical westerly jet streams.
  • Jet Streams and Climate Change:
    • One potential consequence of climate change on jet streams is their potential weakening in strength. As the Arctic region experiences accelerated warming compared to other parts of the globe, the temperature contrast between the Arctic and lower latitudes diminishes. Since the movement of jet streams is driven by these temperature variations, a less pronounced gradient can lead to jet streams that are weaker and exhibit more meandering paths. This phenomenon can result in
PDF p.127

prolonged periods of certain weather conditions, such as heatwaves, coldwaves, droughts, or heavy rainfall.

    • Furthermore, the altered temperature differentials may induce shifts in the positioning of jet streams. As they migrate closer to the poles or display more erratic trajectories, they can exert influence on the trajectories of storms and weather systems. Consequently, this can bring about alterations in precipitation distribution, storm intensity, and the frequency of extreme weather occurrences. Heat Dome Effect:
  • A heat dome refers to a weather phenomenon characterized by

the trapping of hot air beneath a dome of high pressure in the atmosphere. This leads to

prolonged periods of extremely hot temperatures and stifling

conditions, particularly during the summer months.

  • Formation: Heat domes typically form when a large, stagnant area of high pressure settles over a region , causing the air beneath it to sink and compress . As the air descends, it warms up due to compression, creating a dome of hot air near the surface.
  • Consequences: The Heat Dome effect can result in dangerously high temperatures, heatwaves, and heat-related illnesses such as heat exhaustion and heatstroke. Prolonged exposure to extreme heat can also impact agriculture, infrastructure, and energy demand .
  • Regional Variability: Most common in regions with continental climates . Also since Jet Streams have a role in creating these Heat Domes, they are mostly found in Middle or higher latitudes.
  • Climate Change: Climate change is expected to increase the frequency, intensity, and duration of heat domes in many regions, exacerbating the risk of heat-related impacts and challenging efforts to adapt to a warming climate.

DANA (Depresion Aislada en Niveles Altos) Isolated Depression at high levels/Cut-off Low

PDF p.128

Polar Vortex

  • Cold air trapped in its place due to Polar Jet Stream .
  • Can be in both the poles , but impact on human life is mainly due to the North pole vortex .
  • Due to global warming & Arctic Ampliﬁcation and resultant

meandering of the Jet streams, this parcel of cold air can intrude in the non-polar, lower latitudes, causing extremely

cold conditions.

Stratospheric Cooling Stratospheric cooling refers to the gradual decrease in temperature in the stratosphere , primarily due to human-induced changes like

greenhouse gas emissions and ozone depletion. 1. Greenhouse Gas Effect

(Counterintuitive Cooling)

  • Greenhouse gases (especially CO₂) trap heat in the troposphere , warming the lower

atmosphere.

  • However, in the stratosphere , CO₂ acts differently, it radiates heat away into space.
    • CO₂ molecules absorb infrared (IR) radiation and then re-emit it in all directions .
    • In the dense troposphere , that emitted energy often gets reabsorbed by other molecules , keeping heat trapped (warming effect).
    • But in the thin stratosphere , there are fewer molecules to absorb that radiation.
    • Because the stratosphere is less dense and lies higher in the atmosphere, much of

the IR radiation emitted by CO₂ simply escapes into space .

  • As more CO₂ accumulates, the stratosphere loses more heat , causing it to cool down . 2. Ozone Layer Depletion
  • Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs UV radiation , releasing heat and maintaining stratospheric temperature.
  • Due to CFCs and other ozone-depleting substances, the ozone layer thins , especially over the poles.
  • With less ozone , there is less UV absorption , leading to less heating and hence cooling. Anthropogenic greenhouse gases began affecting the stratosphere by ~1885, ﬁve decades

before the detection of CO₂'s impact on tropospheric warming. IMPACT:

  • Slows Ozone Layer Recovery
    • Cooling reduces chemical reaction rates needed to rebuild ozone , delaying ozone layer recovery.
    • Polar Stratospheric Clouds (PSCs) form more readily in cold conditions, which enhance ozone depletion , especially over Antarctica.
  • Strengthens the Polar Vortex
    • A cooler stratosphere intensiﬁes the polar vortex , a band of strong westerly winds circling the poles.
    • This can trap cold air over polar regions or, when destabilized, lead to cold outbreaks in mid-latitudes (e.g., North America, Europe).
  • Disrupts Jet Streams and Weather Patterns
    • Changes in the thermal structure of the stratosphere can shift jet streams , impacting storm tracks , monsoons , and mid-latitude cyclones .
  • Extreme Weather Events
    • This vertical temperature gradient between the stratosphere and troposphere (due to global warming) can enhance convection and influence weather extremes .
  • Affects Aviation and Satellite Orbits
    • Temperature and density changes in the upper atmosphere can alter aircraft flight performance and affect satellite drag , impacting orbital lifetimes.
  • Key Indicator of Climate Change
PDF p.129
    • The simultaneous tropospheric warming and stratospheric cooling is a distinct ﬁngerprint of anthropogenic climate change , not caused by solar activity or natural variability.

  • These are seasonal winds that are experienced in the tropical regions of the world . The most peculiar part about these winds is the reversal they experience with the switch in the apparent positioning of the sun.

10 · HUMIDITY & CONDENSATION#

  • Humidity refers to the amount of water vapor present in the air. It is a measure of the moisture content of the atmosphere and plays a signiﬁcant role in determining weather and climate conditions.
  • There are several different types of humidity:
    • Absolute Humidity : Absolute humidity is the actual amount of water vapor present in a unit volume of air , typically expressed in grams per cubic meter (g/m³). It provides a direct measure of the moisture content of the air.
    • Relative Humidity : Relative humidity is the ratio of the amount of water vapor present in the air to the maximum amount of water vapor that the air can hold at a given temperature , expressed as a percentage . It indicates how close the air is to saturation and is commonly used to describe how "humid" or "muggy" the air feels.
    • Speciﬁc Humidity : Speciﬁc humidity is the ratio of the mass of water vapor to the total mass of air (including dry air and water vapor) in a sample of air. It is expressed in grams of water vapor per kilogram of air and provides a measure of the actual moisture content of the air without regard to temperature.
  • Condensation is the process by which water vapor in the air transforms into liquid water . There are several types of condensation, including:
    • Dew : Dew forms when the surface temperature of an object, such as grass or car windows, falls below the dew point temperature of the surrounding air. Water vapor in the air condenses onto the cooler surface, forming small droplets of liquid water .
      • Dew Point: Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated with water vapor and condensation begins to form. It is a measure of how much moisture is present in the air and is often used as an indicator of comfort level, with lower dew points indicating drier air and higher dew points indicating more humid air.
    • Fog : Fog is a type of condensation that occurs when moist air cools and reaches its dew point, causing water vapor to condense into tiny water droplets suspended in the air near the ground. Fog reduces visibility and is commonly observed in low-lying areas, near bodies of water, or during temperature inversions. Fogs are near-surface clouds.
    • Clouds : Clouds are large masses of water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the atmosphere. They form when moist air rises, cools, and reaches its dew point, causing water vapor to condense onto tiny particles called condensation nuclei. Clouds play a crucial role in the Earth's climate system and weather patterns.
    • Frost : Frost forms when water vapor in the air undergoes deposition, transitioning directly from a gas to a solid without passing through the liquid phase. Frost forms on surfaces such as grass, leaves, or windows when the surface temperature falls below the frost point temperature of the surrounding air.
  • Smog :
    • Smog = smoke + fog (smoky fog) caused by the burning of large amounts of coal, vehicular emission, and industrial fumes (Primary pollutants).
    • Smog contains soot particulates like smoke, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, and other components.
    • At least two distinct types of smog are recognized: sulphurous smog and photochemical smog.
  • Haze: An atmospheric phenomenon where dust, smoke, and other dry particles obscure the clarity of the sky. ATMOSPHERIC RIVERS
  • Atmospheric Rivers are long, narrow corridors of concentrated moisture (water vapour) in the atmosphere. Sometimes they can carry more water than the Amazon River. They are responsible for transporting vast amounts of water vapor from tropical regions to
PDF p.131

mid-latitudes (under the impact of Westerlies), often leading to heavy rainfall and flooding.

  • Creation of Atmospheric Rivers:
    • Evaporation: Warm ocean waters, particularly in tropical regions, cause large-scale evaporation, adding signiﬁcant moisture to the atmosphere.
    • Transport by Wind: Strong winds in the atmosphere, especially within the jet streams, transport this moisture in narrow bands. These winds can extend over thousands of kilometers.
    • Convergence and Condensation: When these moisture-laden air currents encounter mountains or cooler air masses, the moisture condenses into clouds and precipitation, often leading to intense rainfall.

TYPES OF CLOUDS

  • Clouds are categorized into different types based on their altitude, appearance, and the processes that form them. Based on altitude, clouds are generally

classiﬁed into three main categories:

    • High-Level Clouds

(Cirrus Clouds) : These clouds typically form at altitudes above 6,000

meters. They are

composed of ice crystals and appear thin, wispy, and feathery. Examples include cirrus,

cirrostratus, and

cirrocumulus clouds.

    • Mid-Level Clouds (Alto Clouds) : Mid-level clouds typically form between 2,000 to 6,000 meters above the ground. They are composed of water droplets and sometimes ice crystals . Examples include altocumulus and altostratus clouds.
    • Low-Level Clouds : These clouds form at altitudes below 2,000 meters . They are composed of water droplets and are often associated with weather phenomena such as rain or drizzle. Examples include stratus, stratocumulus, and nimbostratus clouds.
  • Additionally, some clouds form vertically through the troposphere , extending through multiple altitude levels:
    • Cumulonimbus Clouds : These towering clouds extend vertically through the troposphere and are associated with thunderstorms, heavy rain, lightning, and sometimes hail and tornadoes.

Polar Stratospheric Clouds

Polar stratospheric clouds (PSCs) form in the stratosphere at altitudes of 15-25 kilometers in polar regions during the winter months , where temperatures drop below -78°C . Typically, clouds do not form in the stratosphere because it is usually too dry and stable; however, the extreme cold in polar regions during winter allows PSCs to form. Often called nacreous or mother-of-pearl clouds due to their iridescent colors, PSCs appear bright and colorful during twilight. PSCs play a critical role in ozone depletion by providing surfaces for chemical reactions that release ozone-depleting chlorine and

PDF p.132

bromine, signiﬁcantly contributing to the formation of the ozone hole over Antarctica. Cloud Seeding Cloud seeding is a type of weather modiﬁcation technique where certain substances are introduced into clouds to stimulate rainfall or snowfall. Process

  • Substances like Silver Iodide (AgI), Potassium Iodide, Sodium Chloride (common salt), or Dry Ice (solid CO₂) are dispersed into clouds.
  • These act as Hygroscopic Nuclei .
  • Water vapor condenses/freezes around them, forming larger droplets or ice crystals.
  • These eventually grow heavy enough to fall as rain or snow. Methods of Delivery
  • Aircrafts : release particles directly into target clouds.
  • Ground-based generators : shoot particles upward using rockets or flares. Applications
  • Enhancing rainfall in drought-prone regions.
  • Increasing snowpack for water supply in mountains.
  • Dispersing fog at airports for visibility.
  • Hail suppression in agriculture by reducing hailstone size.
  • Pollution Control Limitations & Concerns
  • Works only if there is moisture in the air .
  • Effectiveness is variable and debated.
  • Environmental concerns over silver iodide accumulation .
  • Expensive and logistically complex.

TYPES OF PRECIPITATION

  • Precipitation occurs when

water droplets in clouds

coalesce and grow large

enough to overcome air

resistance and fall to the ground . Raindrops form

through the process of

collision and coalescence or the freezing of supercooled water droplets at high

altitudes.

  • Convective (Convectional)

Precipitation:

    • Occurs when the air near the Earth's surface is heated, becomes buoyant, and rises rapidly, forming cumulus clouds that grow into towering cumulonimbus clouds.
    • Intense and localized, often resulting in heavy showers, thunderstorms, and short-lived periods of rainfall.
    • Latitudes: Primarily found in tropical regions near the equator (0° to 30° latitude).
    • Precipitation: Rainfall is the most common type of precipitation associated with convective rainfall. It is these clouds that produce thunderstorms and can also produce hail in some cases.
  • Orographic Precipitation :
    • Forms when moist air is forced to rise over elevated terrain such as mountains or hills.
    • As the air rises , it cools and condenses , leading to the formation of clouds and precipitation on the windward side of the mountain.
    • The leeward side of the mountain may experience a rain shadow effect , with drier conditions and less precipitation.
    • Latitudes: Orographic rainfall can occur at various latitudes but is most common in regions with mountainous terrain.
PDF p.133
    • Precipitation: Rainfall is the typical outcome of orographic lifting. However, at higher elevations and colder temperatures, precipitation can fall as snow . In some cases it can also fall as hail .
  • Frontal (Cyclonic) Precipitation:
    • Occurs along the leading edge of a frontal boundary between two contrasting air masses , such as a cold front or warm front.
    • Warm air is lifted over denser, cooler air, leading to the formation of clouds and

precipitation.

    • Can result in prolonged periods of rainfall over a large area in case of warm front, and short periods of intense rainfall in case of cold fronts.
    • Often associated with mid-latitude cyclones and frontal systems.
    • Latitudes: Frontal rainfall is common in mid-latitude regions (30° to 60° latitude), where contrasting air masses meet.
    • Precipitation: Rainfall is the primary type of precipitation associated with frontal systems. However, in colder regions or during transitional seasons, precipitation can fall as snow or sleet .
  • Cyclonic Precipitation:
    • This is convectional/frontal rainfall on a large scale.
    • Associated with the circulation of air around a low-pressure system, such as a tropical cyclone or extratropical cyclone.
    • Intense and widespread, with heavy rainfall occurring over large areas for an extended period.
    • Can result in flooding, landslides, and other severe weather impacts.
    • Precipitation:
      • Tropical cyclones typically produce heavy rainfall , sometimes accompanied by thunderstorms and hail .
      • In colder regions, extratropical cyclones can result in snowfall.

THUNDERSTORMS:

  • Thunderstorms are atmospheric disturbances characterized by the presence of thunder and lightning, often accompanied by heavy rain, strong winds, and sometimes hail.
  • Formation:
    • Thunderstorms typically form in warm, moist air masses where there is instability and upward vertical motion, of air. This upward motion, i.e. convection (updraft) leads to the

development of

towering cumulonimbus clouds.

  • Stages: Thunderstorms go through three main stages: the cumulus stage, the mature stage, and the

dissipating stage.

    • During the cumulus

stage , warm, moist air rises and forms

cumulus clouds .

    • In the mature stage , updrafts and downdrafts within the cumulonimbus cloud lead to the development of lightning, thunder, heavy rain, and sometimes hail .
    • Finally, in the dissipating stage, the storm weakens as downdrafts dominate and the supply of warm, moist air diminishes.
  • The cumulo nimbus clouds have a large amount of rain drops and ice crystals these particles constantly collide with each other and get charged the lighter positive charges accumulated at the top of clouds while heavier negative charges accumulate at the cloud bottom due to the accumulation of charges at cloud bottom a potential difference (voltage) appears to get created between the ground and the cloud bottom. Initially the air between the cloud and the ground act as an insulator, preventing the passage of any current. However as the potential difference between the cloud and the grounds keeps
PDF p.134

on increasing the current starts to move through the air exciting the nitrogen and oxygen molecules thus creating a bluish/ purpulish glow called lightning full stop the sound associated with this lightning discharge is called as thunder. Apart from ground and clouds the lightning discharge can also occur:

    • Within a

cloud (top

and bottom)

    • Between the clouds
  • The taller objects on the ground (building/trees etc) have a high probability of

experiencing a

lightning event,

as they are

closer to the

cloud bottom. To prevent lightning from destroying the electrical system of a building and endangering the life of the people inside, electric conductors are installed at the top of buildings.

  • Clouds in Thunderstorms:
    • The main cloud type associated with thunderstorms is the cumulonimbus cloud, which is tall and vertically developed. These clouds can reach heights of up to 10 miles (16 kilometers) or more and are characterized by their anvil-shaped tops. Other cloud types, such as cumulus clouds and stratocumulus clouds, may also be present during the early stages of thunderstorm development.
  • Hazards:
    • Thunderstorms can pose various hazards, including lightning strikes , which can cause ﬁres and electrical damage, heavy rainfall leading to flash flooding, strong winds capable of causing property damage and power outages, and hail , which can damage crops, vehicles, and buildings.

TORNADO

  • A tornado is a violently rotating column of air that extends from a thunderstorm to the ground .
  • It's formed when warm, moist air rises rapidly and meets cooler air, creating a strong updraft. This updraft causes the air to spin, and as it spins faster, it becomes more focused and descends towards the ground. If the rotating air column touches the ground, a tornado is formed.
  • Formation:
    • Thunderstorm Development: Tornadoes form within powerful thunderstorms, often associated with strong updrafts of warm, moist air.
    • Wind Shear: As the warm air rises, it encounters cooler air at higher altitudes. This creates wind shear, a difference in wind speed and direction at different levels in the atmosphere.
    • Rotation: The wind shear causes the rising air column to begin rotating . This rotation can be further intensiﬁed by the Coriolis force .
    • Condensation Funnel: As the air column rotates faster and becomes more focused, it cools and condenses, forming a visible funnel cloud. This funnel can be various colors, including white, gray, or even black depending on the amount of debris it picks up.
  • Tornado Characteristics:
    • Size: Tornadoes can vary greatly in size, ranging from a few feet wide to over a mile.
    • Windspeed: Wind speeds in tornadoes can reach incredible speeds, exceeding 300 kmph in the strongest ones.
    • Duration: Most tornadoes are short-lived , lasting only minutes to tens of minutes. However, some can persist for longer periods.
PDF p.135
    • Damage: Tornadoes can cause signiﬁcant damage due to their high wind speeds , lifting and throwing debris, and even causing structural damage to buildings.
  • Tornadoes can be incredibly destructive, with wind speeds reaching over 300 miles per hour. They are most common in the central United States , particularly in an area known as Tornado Alley, which stretches from Texas to Oklahoma, Kansas, and Nebraska. However, they can occur in many parts of the world, including Europe, Asia, Africa, and Australia.
  • Why the majority in “Tornado Alley”?
    • The majority of tornadoes occur in Tornado Alley in the USA due to the unique convergence of different air masses.
    • Warm, moist air from the Gulf of Mexico meets cold, dry air from Canada (Rockies) and warm, dry air from the southwestern deserts .
    • This convergence creates instability, which, combined with strong wind shear (changes in wind speed and direction with height), leads to the formation of powerful thunderstorms called supercells . These supercells are the primary drivers for the high frequency of tornadoes in Tornado Alley.
    • The geography and flat terrain of the region also help funnel and intensify these weather patterns, making conditions ideal for tornado formation.

WATER SPOUTS

  • A swirling column of air and water droplets that forms over a body of water , typically

resembling a tornado.

  • It occurs when warm, moist air rises rapidly and meets cooler air above , causing the air to spin and create a vortex.
  • Usually less intense than

tornadoes and are most

commonly seen over warm

ocean or lake waters.

  • There are two types:

fair-weather waterspouts, which form in calm conditions and don't usually cause much damage, and tornadic waterspouts , which are more intense and can be dangerous.

11 · PYQ#

Q.1) The seasonal reversal of winds is the typical characteristic of - (2014) (a) Equatorial climate (b) Mediterranean climate (c) Monsoon climate (d) All of the above climates

Answer: C

  • Monsoon is traditionally deﬁned as a seasonal reversing wind accompanied by corresponding changes in precipitation but is now used to describe seasonal changes in atmospheric circulation and precipitation associated with the asymmetric heating of land and sea.
  • A monsoon is a seasonal reversal in wind patterns over a region. The word “monsoon” comes from the Arabic word mausim, meaning “season.” The seasonal wind shift is usually accompanied by a dramatic change in precipitation.
  • Winds that blow for approximately six months from the northeast and six months from the southwest. The most prominent monsoons occur in South Asia, Africa, Australia, and the Paciﬁc coast of Central America.
PDF p.136

Q.2) Consider the following statements 1. The winds that blow between 30 degrees N and 60 degrees S latitudes throughout the year are known as westerlies. 2. The moist air masses that cause winter rains in the North-Western region of India are part of westerlies. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (2015) (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2

Answer: B

  • The westerlies, anti-trades, or prevailing westerlies, are prevailing winds from the west toward the east in the middle latitudes between 30 and 60 degrees latitude.
  • They originate from the high-pressure areas in the horse latitudes and trend towards the poles and steer extratropical cyclones in this general manner.
  • Tropical cyclones which cross the subtropical ridge axis into the westerlies recurve due to the increased westerly flow.
  • Westerly disturbances originate in the Mediterranean sea, this sea is surrounded on all sides by high mountains and plateau, as the result high pressure is developed there in the month of September- October, while low pressure still developed over the Mediterranean water body.
  • This disturbance is dragged to India or brought to India by the Jet stream (westerly winds (flowing west to east)).
  • This is the reason that J&K and NW part of India receives highest rainfall from westerly disturbances.

Q.3) In the context of which of the following do some scientists suggest the use of cirrus cloud thinning technique and the injection of sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere? (2019) (a) Creating the artiﬁcial rains in some regions (b) Reducing the frequency and intensity of tropical cyclones (c) Reducing the adverse effects of solar wind on the Earth (d) Reducing global warming

Answer: D

  • Cirrus clouds do not reflect a lot of solar radiation back into space, but because they form at high altitudes and cold temperatures, they trap long-wave radiation and have a climate impact similar to greenhouse gases.
  • Thus Thinning cirrus clouds would reduce the absorption of infrared radiation and proposed a form of climate engineering to reduce global warming.
  • Another proposed Geo-engineering technique involves injecting reflective sulphate aerosol particles into Earth’s lower stratosphere to cast a small proportion of the inbound sunlight back into space and cool the planet off.
  • Thus both are climate engineering/ Geo-engineering techniques to reduce global warming.

Q.4) Why are dewdrops not formed on a cloudy night? (2019) (a) Clouds absorb the radiation released from the Earth’s surface. (b) Clouds reflect back the Earth’s radiation. (c) The Earth’s surface would have low temperature on cloudy nights. (d) Clouds deflect the blowing wind to ground level.

Answer: B

  • Less dew is formed on cloudy nights because radiation during cloudy nights occurs at a very slow pace.
PDF p.137
  • The radiation occurs very slowly because the clouds are thick during cloudy nights and trap the heat and water vapour inside the clouds.
  • All this indicates why the level of dew is reduced during nights that are heavy with clouds.
  • Dew is a natural form of water, formed as water vapour condenses. Dew, like the glistening drop on this grassy ﬁeld in Anaconda, Montana, forms as water near the surface of the ground is cooled to its dew point, the temperature at which water vapour condenses. When the sky is cloudy, the trees and plants do not get cool in the night and hence there is less dew formation because on a cloudy night, the clouds send the heat (earth's radiation) back to the ground so the ground never gets cold enough for the dew to be formed.

Q.5) Consider the following statements: 1. Jet streams occur in the Northern Hemisphere only. 2. Only some cyclones develop an eye. 3. The temperature inside the eye of a cyclone is nearly 10°C lesser than that of the surroundings. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (2020) (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 2 only (d) 1 and 3 only

Answer: C

  • Jet streams occur in both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. The actual appearance of jet streams result from the complex interaction between many variables - such as the location of high and low pressure systems, warm and cold air, and seasonal changes. Statement 1 is incorrect.
  • The warmest part of Erin's eye was almost 21 degrees (Fahrenheit) warmer than the surrounding air, a dramatic difference from the air around it. Above 7.5 miles high, the eye's temperature dropped quickly to the same temperature as the air outside the eye. Statement 3 is incorrect.

Q.6) Consider the following statements: 1. High clouds primarily reflect solar radiation and cool the surface of the Earth. 2. Low clouds have a high absorption of infrared radiation emanating from the Earth's surface and thus cause warming effect. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (2022) (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2

Answer: D

  • High clouds are often thin and do not reflect very much. They let lots of the Sun's warmth in. They radiate less energy into space than the lower, warmer clouds.

Therefore, high clouds work to "trap" more energy than the low clouds.

  • Low clouds are often quite thick and reflect lots of sunlight back to space. Low clouds are excellent reflectors. But, they don't stop the longwave energy from escaping to space. Therefore, low clouds help to cool the Earth.
