12 · AIR MASSES#

  • When the air remains over a homogenous area for a sufﬁciently longer time, it acquires the characteristics of the area.
  • This air parcel with distinctive homogeneous characteristics in terms of temperature and humidity is called an air mass.
  • Due to these homogenous conditions, they lack any vertical movement of winds within themselves.
  • The homogenous regions can be the vast ocean surface or vast plains and plateaus.
  • Air masses form an integral part of the global planetary wind system. Therefore, they are associated with one or other wind belts.
  • They extend from the surface to the lower stratosphere and are across thousands of kilometers. This is why the Jet streams can carry them from their source location to other places.
  • Source Region:
    • They are often the places where the wind movement is absent so that the air can stay at the same place for a longer period of time, resulting in the uniform transfer of the land characteristics to the air.
    • That is why the source regions are High-Pressure regions that experience atmospheric stability.
    • The main source regions are the high-pressure belts in the subtropics (giving rise to tropical air masses) and around the poles (the source for polar air masses):
      • Warm tropical and subtropical oceans
      • The subtropical hot deserts
      • The relatively cold high-latitude oceans
      • The very cold snow-covered continents in high latitudes
      • Permanently ice-covered continents in the Arctic and Antarctica
    • Tropical air masses are warm, while polar air masses are cold.
    • Continental Air masses are dry while maritime ones are with moisture.
    • When an air mass moves away from a source region, the upper level maintains the physical characteristics for a longer period.
    • This is possible because air masses are stable with stagnant air which does not facilitate convection.
    • Conduction and radiation in such stagnant air are not effective.
  • Major Air Masses:
    • Maritime tropical (mT)
    • Continental tropical (cT)
    • Maritime polar (mP)
    • Continental polar (cP)
    • Continental Arctic (cA)
  • Climatic Impact of Air Masses:
    • Tropical (T): Warm temperatures.
      • Maritime Tropical (mT): Warm, moist air from tropical oceans.
  • Brings heavy rainfall and thunderstorms to coastal regions and mid-latitudes , and contributes to tropical cyclones and hurricanes.
  • Southeast Asia: The maritime tropical air masses from the South China Sea cause signiﬁcant rainfall during the wet season, contributing to the region's lush tropical climate.
  • Amazon Basin: The mT air mass from the Atlantic Ocean brings abundant rainfall, supporting the Amazon rainforest ecosystem.
      • Continental Tropical (cT): Hot, dry air from desert regions.
  • Impact: Causes heatwaves and dry conditions in continental interiors , influences summer climates in regions like the southwestern USA.
  • Sahara Desert: The hot, dry cT air mass dominates, leading to extremely high temperatures and arid conditions.
PDF p.140
  • Central Australia: The interior experiences hot, dry conditions due to the influence of cT air masses, resulting in arid and semi-arid climates.
    • Polar (P): Cold temperatures, can vary in humidity.
      • Maritime Polar (mP): Cool, moist air from high-latitude oceans.
  • Brings cool, damp, and cloudy weather with precipitation to coastal and inland regions , particularly in the winter.
  • Western Europe: The mP air mass from the North Atlantic Ocean brings cool, moist conditions, resulting in frequent rain and cloudy weather, especially in the UK and Ireland.
  • Japan: The Sea of Japan coast experiences cold, snowy winters due to mP air masses from the Sea of Okhotsk.
      • Continental Polar (cP): Cold, dry air from high-latitude land areas.
  • Causes cold, dry conditions in winter , can lead to clear, cold weather and influence winter storm tracks in mid-latitudes .
  • Russia (Siberia): cP air masses from the interior lead to extremely cold, dry winters with clear skies and very low temperatures.
  • Canada (Prairies): The influence of cP air masses results in cold, dry winters with clear skies, contributing to the region's continental climate.
    • Arctic (A): Extremely cold, very dry.
      • Continental Arctic (cA): Very cold, dry air from Arctic regions.
  • Brings frigid temperatures and clear skies , influences polar vortex events and can push cold air far into mid-latitudes, causing severe winter weather.
  • Northern Canada and Greenland: cA air masses bring extremely cold, dry conditions, influencing the Arctic climate and contributing to polar vortex events that can push cold air southward.
  • Scandinavia: Periodic invasions of cA air masses can cause severe cold spells and harsh winter weather.
    • Equatorial (E): Very warm, very humid.
      • Maritime Equatorial (mE): Extremely warm and moist air from equatorial oceans.
  • Contributes to heavy rainfall and thunderstorms in equatorial regions , influences monsoon climates and enhances tropical cyclone development.
  • Indonesia and Malaysia: The mE air mass brings high humidity and signiﬁcant rainfall, supporting the region's tropical rainforest climate.
  • West Africa (Gulf of Guinea): The mE air mass contributes to heavy rainfall and the humid tropical climate of the coastal regions.
    • Overall Impacts on Global Climate:
      • Temperature Regulation: Air masses redistribute heat globally, balancing temperature differences between the equator and poles.
      • Precipitation Patterns: Maritime air masses (mT, mP) bring moisture and precipitation, impacting rainfall patterns and water availability.
      • Weather Systems and Storms: Interactions between different air masses lead to the formation of weather fronts, cyclones, and storms, influencing weather patterns and extremes.
      • Seasonal Variations: The movement of air masses with seasons contributes to seasonal climate variations, such as monsoons and winter storms.

FRONTS

  • These are the 3-dimensional boundary zones , between 2 air masses of contrasting characteristics .
  • They are typically found in the mid-latitudinal regions , and are uncommon in tropics and the polar regions.
  • The process of formation of a front is known as Frontogenesis (the war/face-off begins), and the dissipation of a front is known as Frontolysis (one of the air masses wins, and the war is now over).
  • The temperate cyclone owe their genesis to the process of frontogenesis.
  • Characteristics of Fronts:
PDF p.141
    • The more the temperature contrast between the 2 air masses, the lesser the thickness of the front formed.
    • With a sudden change in temperature through the front, there is a change in pressure also.
    • Sudden wind shifts too.
    • The zone experiences precipitation due to the upliftment (gradual or forced) of the warm air.
    • The cold air masses and fronts moves faster than the warm front as the compact and denser cold air can push the boundaries with more force.
  • Types of Fronts:
    • Stationary Front:
      • Forms when two air masses meet but neither advances signiﬁcantly.
      • Clouds: A mix of stratocumulus, nimbostratus, and altostratus.
      • Clouds and light precipitation can persist along a stationary front for an extended period.
    • Warm Front:
      • Forms when a warm air mass advancesinto the region of a cold air mass.
      • Clouds: Stratus, altostratus, cirrostratus.
      • These clouds often produce steady rain or drizzle and can lead to overcast skies and fog.
    • Cold Front:
      • Forms when a cold air mass advances and displaces a warm air mass.
      • Clouds: Cumulus, towering cumulonimbus.
      • These clouds often produce thunderstorms, heavy rain, hail, and tornadoes.
    • Occluded Front:
      • Forms when a fast-moving cold front overtakes a slower-moving warm front.
      • Clouds: A mix of cumulus, stratocumulus, and nimbostratus.
      • Can produce a variety of weather conditions , including thunderstorms, rain, and cooler temperatures as warm air is lifted off the surface.
      • Warm Occlusion:
  • Forms when a fast-moving cold front overtakes a slower-moving warm front, and the air ahead of the warm front is cooler than the air behind the cold front.
  • Warm air is lifted off the surface, creating a mix of clouds, including cumulus, stratocumulus, and nimbostratus.
PDF p.142
  • Typically associated with moderate to heavy precipitation, including rain and sometimes thunderstorms.
  • The warm sector ahead of the occluded front may experience warmer temperatures compared to the cold sector behind it.
      • Cold Occlusion:
  • Forms when a fast-moving cold front overtakes a slower-moving warm front, but the air behind the cold front is colder than the air ahead of the warm front.
  • Cold air wedges underneath the warm air, lifting it off the surface.
  • Clouds: A mix of stratocumulus, nimbostratus, and altostratus.
  • Typically associated with widespread precipitation, including rain or snow, and cooler temperatures. A mix of cold & warm front weathers.
  • The resulting weather can be like that of a warm occlusion but with colder temperatures and a greater likelihood of snow in the colder air mass.
PDF p.143

13 · CYCLONES#

  • Cyclones are large-scale atmospheric systems characterized by low-pressure centers and circulating winds that rotate counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
  • There are different types of cyclones, including tropical cyclones, extratropical cyclones, and subtropical cyclones.
  • Tropical cyclones, also known as hurricanes or typhoons depending on the region, form over tropical or subtropical waters and are characterized by intense thunderstorms and strong winds.
  • Extratropical cyclones form outside the tropics and are associated with frontal systems and changes in temperature gradients.

TROPICAL CYCLONES:

  • Location:
    • Tropical cyclones primarily occur in tropical and subtropical regions over warm ocean waters, typically between 10° and 30° latitude in both hemispheres.
    • They are known as Cyclones in the Indian Ocean, Hurricanes in the Atlantic, Typhoons in the Western Paciﬁc and South China Sea, and Willy-willies in Western Australia.
  • Necessary Conditions:
    • Warm Ocean Waters: Sea surface temperatures of at least 26.5°C (80°F) are necessary to fuel tropical cyclone development.
    • Moisture: High levels of atmospheric moisture are essential for sustaining convective activity and cloud formation.
    • Low Vertical Wind Shear: Minimal change in wind speed and direction with height allows for vertical development of the storm.
  • Formation:
    • A disturbance , such as a low pressure centre like monsoon trough, serves as the initial seed for tropical cyclone development.
    • If the atmospheric and oceanic conditions are favourable, the disturbance may undergo cyclogenesis , the process by which a tropical cyclone forms. Warm, moist air rises rapidly, creating an area of low pressure at the surface. As the air converges and rises, it cools and condenses, releasing latent heat and further fuelling the convective activity.
    • As the disturbance intensiﬁes and becomes better organized, it may develop into a tropical depression, characterized by a closed circulation and maximum sustained winds of up to 38 miles per hour (62 kilometres per hour).
    • If the conditions persist, the depression continues to strengthen into a cyclone.
    • Once formed, tropical cyclones can track across the ocean and intensify, fuelled by warm ocean waters and favourable atmospheric conditions. They may reach their peak intensity at some point before eventually weakening as they move over cooler waters or make landfall.
PDF p.144
  • Structure:
    • Eye: A well-deﬁned center of low pressure characterized by calm winds and clear skies.
    • Eyewall: A ring of intense thunderstorms surrounding the eye, where the strongest winds and heaviest rainfall occur.
    • Rainbands: Bands of clouds and thunderstorms extending outward from the center, bringing additional rainfall and gusty winds.
  • Types of Clouds Associated:
    • Cumulonimbus Clouds: Towering clouds with strong updrafts and potential for severe weather, including heavy rainfall, lightning, and hail.
    • Cirrus Clouds: High-altitude clouds that may indicate the presence of upper-level outflow associated with the storm.
  • Impact:
    • Strong Winds: Tropical cyclones can produce sustained winds of 64 knots (74 mph) or greater, capable of causing widespread damage to structures, vegetation, and infrastructure.
    • Heavy Rainfall: Intense rainfall can lead to flooding, landslides, and mudslides, especially in areas with poor drainage or in mountainous terrain.
    • Storm Surge: The onshore flow of water driven by strong winds can result in storm surges, causing coastal flooding and inundation of low-lying areas.
    • Tornadoes: Embedded within rainbands, tornadoes can form and cause additional localized damage.
    • Economic and Humanitarian Impacts: Tropical cyclones can result in loss of life, displacement of populations, disruption of essential services, and signiﬁcant economic losses.

TEMPERATE CYCLONES

  • Location:
    • Temperate cyclones, also

known as

extratropical cyclones, occur in the

mid-latitudes, typically between 30°

and 60° latitude in both

hemispheres.

    • They are most common in

regions with a strong temperature contrast between polar and tropical air masses , such as North America, Europe, and Asia.

  • Necessary Conditions:
    • Temperature Contrast: A signiﬁcant temperature difference between polar and tropical air masses is essential for the development of temperate cyclones.
    • Baroclinic Instability: The interaction between warm and cold air masses along a frontal boundary creates instability, leading to the formation of cyclones.
  • Formation:
    • Temperate cyclones form along frontal boundaries, where warm and cold air masses meet and create a zone of instability.
    • The process begins with the development of a stationary front, where warm air rises over denser, cooler air.
    • As the temperature gradient steepens and instability increases, a low-pressure system forms and begins to intensify.
PDF p.145
  • Structure:
    • Warm and Cold Fronts:

Temperate cyclones are

associated with both warm and cold fronts, which mark the leading edges of

advancing air masses.

    • Cyclonic Rotation: In the Northern Hemisphere ,

temperate cyclones rotate counterclockwise around

their centers, while in the Southern Hemisphere , they rotate clockwise.

    • Occluded Front: As the

cyclone matures, the cold front catches up to the warm front, resulting in an occluded front and the eventual dissipation of the cyclone.

  • Types of Clouds Associated:
    • Cumulonimbus Clouds: Towering clouds associated with thunderstorms and heavy rainfall, especially along the cold front.
    • Nimbostratus Clouds: Layered clouds that produce steady rain or snow, often associated with the warm sector of the cyclone.
    • Altostratus Clouds: Mid-level clouds that may precede the warm front and bring overcast conditions and light precipitation.
  • Impact:
    • Precipitation: Temperate cyclones can produce a variety of precipitation types, including rain, snow, sleet, and freezing rain, depending on temperature and atmospheric conditions.
    • Strong Winds: Gusty winds associated with the cyclone can cause damage to structures, trees, and power lines.
    • Flooding: Heavy rainfall from temperate cyclones can lead to flash flooding, river flooding, and landslides.
    • Storm Surge: Along coastal areas, the onshore flow of water driven by strong winds can result in storm surges and coastal flooding.

IMPACT OF CLIMATE CHANGE

Tropical Cyclones:

  • Rising ocean temperatures due to climate change provide more energy for tropical cyclones, leading to more intense storms with higher wind speeds and heavier rainfall. There has been an increase in the proportion of severe (Category 4 & 5) cyclones, especially in regions like the Arabian Sea and the North Atlantic.
  • Climate models show a decreased overall frequency of tropical cyclones globally, with some regions like the North Atlantic bucking the trend by becoming slightly more active.
  • The cyclones are encroaching even higher latitudes (poleward shift), and their forward motion has slowed down, which can prolong rainfall and increase flood risks.
  • Climate change leads to an increase in rapid intensiﬁcation events (storms that quickly strengthen), making forecasts and disaster responses more difﬁcult.
  • Sea level rise exacerbates storm surges from cyclones, increasing coastal flooding hazards. Temperate Cyclones:
  • Temperate cyclones (also called extratropical cyclones or mid-latitude storms) may experience shifts in their tracks due to climate change, often moving poleward (lack of availability of cold air masses at lower latitudes), which could alter weather patterns in affected regions.
  • Warming impacts the temperature gradients and jet stream patterns that drive temperate cyclones, potentially modifying their intensity, frequency, and seasonal behavior.
  • Increased atmospheric moisture from climate change can lead to more intense precipitation events associated with these cyclones, enhancing the risks of flooding,
PDF p.146

landslides, and transport disruption. There is evidence of excess rainfall and unseasonal weather in areas affected by temperate cyclones, which can impact crops and infrastructure.

TROPICAL v/s TEMPERATE CYCLONES

Q.1) In the South Atlantic and South Eastern Paciﬁc regions in tropical latitudes, cyclones do not originate. What is the reason? (2015) (a) Sea Surface temperature are low (b) Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone seldom occurs (c) Coriolis force is too weak (d) The absence of land in those regions

Answer: B The most proximate reasons for the lack of cyclone formation in the South Atlantic are sea

PDF p.147

surface temperatures that tend to run a shade cooler than ideal for tropical cyclone formation even in the southern summer, climatologically high values of vertical wind shear across that basin throughout the year, and a lack of pre-existing centres of rotation (vorticity) in that area.

  • Tropical cyclones are the zones of low pressure systems around which there is closed air circulation in counterclockwise direction(Northern hemisphere) and circular

direction(Southern hemisphere).

  • Important condition for the origin of tropical cyclones:
    • Sea Surface temperature should be greater than 27 degree C.
    • Pre existing weak tropical disturbances
    • Continuous supply of energy.
    • Coriolis force.
    • Weak wind shear
  • Strong Wind shear present at South Atlantic removes the heat and moisture from the place where it is required to drive the heat engine of cyclone i.e near the centre.
  • Without an Inter-tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) to provide synoptic vorticity and convergence (i.e large scale spin and thunderstorm activity) as well as having strong wind shear, it becomes very difﬁcult to nearly impossible to have genesis of tropical cyclones.

Q.1) If a tropical rainforest is removed, it does not regenerate quickly as compared to a tropical deciduous forest. This is because - (2011) (a) the soil of rainforest is deﬁcient in nutrients (b) propagules of the trees in a rainforest have poor viability (c) the rain forest species are slow-growing (d) exotic species invade the fertile soil of rainforest

Answer: A Due to heavy rainfall and weathering, most of the nutrients have been washed out of the soil.

  • Only a thin layer of decaying organic matter is found, unlike in temperate deciduous forests.That’s why the soil of most of the tropical rainforest is poor in nutrients.
  • The high temperature and moisture of tropical rainforests cause dead organic matter in the soil to decompose more quickly than in other climates, thus releasing and losing its nutrients rapidly. The high volume of rain in tropical rainforests washes nutrients out of the soil more quickly than in other climates.
  • Why are rainforest soils low in nutrients? One reason the rain forest soil is so poor is that most of the nutrients are stored in the plants themselves. In any forest, dead organic matter falls to the ground, providing valuable nutrients for new growth. In cooler or drier climates, the nutrients build up in the soil.

Q.2) What could be the main reason/reasons for the formation of the African and Eurasian desert belt? 1. It is located in the sub-tropical high-pressure cells. 2. It is under the influence of warm ocean currents. Which of the statements given above is/are correct in this context? (2011) (a) 1 only

PDF p.155

(b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2

Answer: A

  • Hot deserts are located between 20°30° latitude in both the hemisphere on the western coast of the continents.
  • They are also called Tropical Deserts.
  • They are different from the midlatitude deserts and cold deserts, hot deserts are found in High-pressure belts along the Tropics in the trade winds region.
  • Distribution Of Hot Deserts:
    • Asia Thar desert and the Arabian Desert;
    • Africa The Sahara and the Kalahari;
    • N. America Lower California and Arizona states of the USA;
    • S. AmericaAtacama desert;
    • Australia The Great Australian desert.
    • The Sahara desert of Africa is the biggest hot desert in the world.
    • The Hot desert regions are located in the subtropical high-pressure belts, which are not favourable regions for rainfall.
    • There are three main causes of deserts:
      • Most of the world's deserts are made by the equatorial wind belts.
      • At the equator, warm air is always rising.
      • This creates wind belts that blow north and south away from the equator.
    • When air descends at the tropics of cancer and Capricorn it is too dry for clouds to form.
    • No clouds mean no rain producing Deserts. E.g. the Sahara desert
    • Rainshadow also produces Deserts.
    • Any moisture in the air will fall as air passes high mountain ranges, so land beyond the mountains receives little or no rain.
    • The Gobi desert is produced by Rainshadow.
    • Cold Currents also produce deserts.
    • The southwestern coast of Africa and South America are swept by cold currents upwelling from the ocean floor. These currents cool the air that passes over them, causing the water in the air to fall as rain before it reaches the land. The Namib and Atacama desert have formed because of these cold currents.

Q.3) Which one of the following is the characteristic climate of the Tropical Savannah Region? (2012) (a) Rainfall throughout the year (b) Rainfall in winter only (c) An extremely short dry season (d) A deﬁnite dry and wet season

Answer: D The tropical savanna climate is also called the tropical wet and dry climate. It is the climate experienced in savanna or tropical grassland regions of the world.

  • These places are located near the equator, and they lie between the Southern and the Northern Tropics.
  • The climate dominates many parts of the African continent, the northern region of South America, and parts of Asia such as India.
  • The tropical savanna climate has alternating dry and wet seasons, hence its name.
  • It shares some similar characteristics with the tropical monsoon climate, but it receives less annual rainfall as compared to the tropical monsoon climate.
PDF p.156
  • Tropical savanna climates are relatively hot since they lie within the tropical latitudes.
  • Precipitation in the tropical savanna climate is mainly in the form of rainfall. On average, this climatic zone receives between 800 and 1,600 millimetres of rain annually.

Q.4) "Each day is more or less the same, the morning is dear and bright with a sea breeze; as the Sun climbs high in the sky, heat mounts up, dark clouds form, then rain comes with thunder and lightning. But rain is soon over". Which of the following regions is described in the above passage? (2015) (a) Savannah (b) Equatorial (c) Monsoon (d) Mediterranean

Answer: B Regions with this climate experience high temperatures all year round.

  • The average monthly temperatures are about 26 – 28 degrees Celsius.
  • The annual temperature range (the difference between the average temperature of the hottest and coldest months) is very small.
  • The annual temperature range may be as low as 3 degrees Celsius.
  • The diurnal or daily temperature range (the difference between the highest temperature in the day and the lowest temperature at night) is usually greater. Humidity is usually very high.
  • Another major characteristic of this climate is high rainfall.
  • These regions usually experience 2000 mm of rainfall or more in a year.
  • Rainfall is high for most of the year.
  • Many equatorial regions are affected by the ITCZ.
  • As the ITCZ passes over these areas it brings heavy rainfall and thunderstorms.
  • In some areas, the ITCZ causes two periods of very heavy rainfall every year.
  • One occurs when the ITCZ crosses these areas on its way north and another occurs when it crosses these areas again on its way south.

Q.5) Which of the following leaf modiﬁcations occur(s) in the desert areas to inhibit water loss? 1. Hard and waxy leaves 2. Tiny leaves 3. Thorns instead of leaves Select the correct answer using the code given below: (2018) (a) 2 and 3 only (b) 2 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3

Answer: D Leaf modiﬁcations of Desert Plant to inhibit water loss for adaptations and survival of Desert Plant-

  • Wax coatings on leaves prevent water loss through transpiration, which in the hot desert can cause loss of water from both the surface and the inside of the leaves. Leaves are also smaller on desert plants, further reducing the possibility for water loss.
  • Deciduous plants in desert ecosystems have adapted through the activity of their leaves. Leaves on these plants are typically smaller and coated with wax to prevent evapo-transpiration.
  • Plants are equipped with fleshy leaves that contain much of their water supply. Because of their moist inner bodies, these plants are called succulents. They typically feel spongy and when cut open are ﬁlled with a pulpy flesh, protected by a waxy outer layer.
PDF p.157
  • Many plants in the desert conserve water by not having any leaves at all. Cacti are the most proliﬁc of this plant type. Many cacti have spines instead of leaves, which conduct photosynthesis and catch dew when the climate is right. These small structures also reflect light, further reducing water loss. During heavy rains, cacti will grow temporary root systems and absorb water. They will then shed the roots when the ground has dried.

Q.6) The vegetation of savannah consists of grassland with scattered small trees. The forest development in such areas is generally kept in check by one or more or a combination of some conditions. Which of the following are such conditions? 1. Burrowing animals and termites 2. Fire 3. Grazing herbivores 4. Seasonal rainfall 5. Soil properties Select the correct answer using the code given below (2021) (a) 1 and2 (b) 4 and 5 (c) 2, 3 and 4 (d) 1, 3 and 5

Answer: C

  • Savanna vegetation includes scrub , grasses and occasional trees, which grow near water holes , seasonal rivers or aquifers . Plants and animals have to adapt to the long dry periods. Many plants are xerophytic - for example, the acacia tree with its small, waxy leaves and thorns.
  • The crops grown in the savanna are mainly annuals, the staple food crops being maize, millets and sorghum, but in many regions cassava is planted as a 'hedge' against crop failure. Cash crops include groundnuts, cotton and, at higher altitudes in East Mrica, coffee.
  • So, the Vegetation is deliberately reduced in size by keeping in mind of the various factors which can play an important role in increasing the growth of the disasters.

Q.7) “Leaf litter decomposes faster than in any other biome and as a result, the soil surface is often almost bare. Apart from trees, the vegetation is largely composed of plant forms that reach up into the canopy vicariously, by climbing the trees or growing as epiphytes, rooted on the upper branches of trees.” This is the most likely description of (2021) (a) Coniferous forest (b) Dry deciduous forest (c) Mangrove forest (d) Tropical rain forest

Answer: D

  • Option d is correct. In tropical rainforest biome, hot, moist atmosphere and all the dead plant material create the perfect conditions in which bacteria and other microorganisms can thrive. This leads to rapid decomposition of leaf litter material. The tropical rainforest is known for its dense canopies of vegetation that form three different layers. The top layer or canopy contains giant trees that grow to heights of 75 m (about 250 ft) or more. Thick, woody vines are also found in the canopy. They climb trees in the canopy to reach for sunlight.

Q.8) Consider the following statements: Statement-I : The soil in tropical rain forests is rich in nutrients. Statement-II : The high temperature and moisture of tropical rain forests cause dead organic matter in the soil to decompose quickly. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? (2023)

PDF p.158

(a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I (b) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I (c) Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect (d) Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct

Answer: D

  • The soil here is not rich in nutrients. It is in fact leached, as the fast growing vegetation constantly keep on absorbing the nutrients being created in the soil.

Q.9) Consider the following description: (2024)

1. Annual and daily range of temperatures is low. 2. Precipitation occurs throughout the year. 3. Precipitation varies between 50 cm – 250 cm. What is this type of climate? (a) Equatorial climate (b) China type climate (c) Humid subtropical climate (d) Marine West coast climate Answer: (d) Marine West coast climate

Q.10) Consider the following statements: Statement I: The amount of dust particles in the atmosphere is more in subtropical and temperate areas than in equatorial and polar regions. Statement II: Subtropical and temperate areas have less dry winds. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? (a) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I (b) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II does not explain Statement I (c) Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct (d) Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct

Answer: (c) Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct Statement I: Correct

  • Dust concentration is higher in subtropical and temperate regions, particularly in arid and semi-arid zones like the Sahara Desert, Arabian Peninsula, Central Asia, and parts of China.
  • These areas have scarce vegetation, high wind activity, and dry conditions, ideal for dust uplift.
  • In contrast, equatorial regions are humid and forested (e.g., Amazon, Congo), limiting dust production. Polar regions are ice-covered, also limiting dust. Statement II: Incorrect
  • Subtropical regions, especially deserts (e.g., Sahara, Thar), experience strong dry winds like:
    • Trade winds
    • Harmattan (West Africa)
    • Santa Ana (California)
  • These dry winds are key agents for transporting dust particles across continents and oceans.
  • Therefore, the statement that these areas have “less dry winds” is factually incorrect.

Quick revise: memory cards, PYQs and alerts#

My condensed layer for this subject, topic by topic: mnemonic cards, PYQ tables with answers and handout alerts.

1 · Atmosphere & heat

🏢 The atmosphere is a 5-floor building (bottom → top)

Floor Height What happens there
5 Exosphere – open terrace > 400 km Particles can reach 1,000 °C yet it feels cold (too thin to pass heat)
4 Thermosphere – rooftop antenna 80–400 km Temperature rises again (UV, X-ray). ISS & satellites; Kármán line 100 km; ionosphere bounces radio waves
3 Mesosphere – freezer 50–80 km Coldest; meteors burn; noctilucent clouds
2 Stratosphere – AC floor to 50 km Ozone (lower part) → temperature rises with height; almost cloud-free = jets fly here
1 Troposphere – kitchen 8–18 km (avg 13) All weather, clouds, jet streams. 18 km at equator (strong convection), 8 km at poles. Cools ~1 °C per 165 m
  • Gases: N₂ 78% · O₂ 21% (≈99%) · Argon 0.93% · CO₂ ~0.04% · water vapour 0–5% (>90% below 5 km; falls from equator to poles) · CO₂ and water vapour only up to 90 km · ozone layer 20–25 km. By composition: homosphere (<80 km, uniform) and heterosphere (>80 km, layered by molecular mass). Aerosols/salt act as hygroscopic nuclei; microplastics can seed ice 5–10 °C warmer than usual.
  • Why cooler with height (PYQ 2012, ans C): air is heated from the ground up and thinner air holds less heat. Not because of "more moisture" (vapour falls with height). Handout also quotes 6.5 °C per 1,000 m (≈ the 1 °C/165 m above).
  • Troposphere – PYQ 2024 (ans a): thicker at the equator because strong convection carries heat high. (Mains 2022, 15m: "troposphere determines weather processes – how?" → clouds, air masses, jet streams all sit here; prime heat source is terrestrial radiation.)
  • CO₂ warms (PYQ 2012, ans D): it absorbs infrared; transparent to incoming sunlight, opaque to outgoing earth radiation. Water vapour also absorbs infrared (2023 ans C).
  • Ionosphere (PYQ 2011, ans D): radio works because charged particles reflect waves – not ozone, and radio waves are not "very long" (1 mm–100 km).
  • Heat budget (PYQ 2024, ans d): the atmosphere is heated more by terrestrial (long-wave) than by incoming (short-wave) radiation, and greenhouse gases absorb long-wave well → only Statement II correct.

🔥 4 ways heat moves: Conduction = Contact (spoon in hot chai) · Convection = Currents (boiling milk rises/sinks) · Advection = Aside, sideways (Loo carrying heat in) · Radiation = Rays, no medium (Sun → Earth). 👕 Albedo: snow/ice = white shirt (reflects, cools) · ocean, forest, city = black shirt (absorbs, warms). Hotter body → shorter wavelength: Sun = short-wave, Earth = long-wave.

What controls temperature: latitude (slant rays) · duration of daylight · sunspot cycle · transparency (cloudy day cooler, cloudy night warmer) · altitude · mountain orientation · vegetation (transpiration cools) · distance from sea · ocean currents · local winds/urban. Energy: 0–40° N/S = surplus; beyond 40° = deficit; winds and currents carry heat poleward, mostly across 30°–50° (hence storms there).

Isotherm bending (PYQs 2024, 2025): January, Northern Hemisphere – isotherms bend poleward over oceans (oceans stay warmer) and equatorward over continents (land cools fast). July is the reverse. Reason: water has high specific heat (2023: Statement I wrong – contrast is greater in winter; Statement II right). Continental interiors have a bigger annual range because of land–water thermal difference only (2013, ans A).

Handout alert: the isotherm section first says "in July isotherms shift towards the equator on land" and then summarises "in July, north over land, south over oceans". Trust the summary (and the Jan rule above).

Temperature inversion: temperature rises with height. Needs clear, calm, long nights, no mixing, valleys/basins; common at fronts, in winter, in mountains and valleys. Good: frost protection. Bad: pollution dome, fog, pests. (Beijing's 2013 US$100-bn drive cut PM2.5 by 35% by 2017.)

2 · Pressure, winds & circulation

🪜 Pressure ladder – "Lazy Hens Lay Happily": Equator Low (ITCZ / Doldrums, 10°N–S) → High at ~30° → Low at ~60° → High at poles. 7 belts = 3 thermal + 4 dynamic. Belts shift 5–10° (up to 25° over India) with the overhead Sun; balanced at the equinoxes (21 Mar, 23 Sep). At 30–40° this shift gives the Mediterranean pattern: winter westerlies = rain; summer dry trades.

Three forces on wind: Pressure gradient (speed + direction; close isobars = fast) · Coriolis (direction only; deflects right in N, left in S; 0 at equator, max at poles; bigger for faster winds – PYQ 2024, ans c) · Friction (both; only a few thousand metres up; less over sea so winds are faster there). Winds are named for where they come from. Types: planetary · geostrophic (above friction, parallel to isobars, e.g. jet streams) · seasonal (monsoon) · diurnal (sea/land breeze, mountain-valley) · local.

Planetary wind From → to Notes
Trade winds subtropical high → equator, easterly helped trade routes; push ocean currents
Westerlies subtropical high → sub-polar low, W→E strongest in S. Hemisphere (little land): Roaring 40s, Furious 50s, Shrieking 60s
Polar easterlies polar high → mid-latitudes cold, weaker

🌀 Three cells: Hadley (equator–30°, biggest, trades) · Ferrel (30–60°, middle, runs opposite) · Polar (60°–pole, smallest, polar easterlies). Hadley Hot, Ferrel Fill-in, Polar Puny.

PYQ 2011 (ans A): Southern westerlies are stronger because the southern hemisphere has less land – not because Coriolis is higher there. PYQ 2015 (ans B): westerlies blow between 30° and 60° (not "30°N to 60°S") and bring NW India's winter rain (western disturbances).

Jet streams & friends

  • Jet streams: narrow fast bands at 8–15 km. Permanent: Polar (50–60°, strongest in winter) and Subtropical (20–30°). Temporary: Tropical Easterly, Somali. Occur in both hemispheres (PYQ 2020: "Northern only" is wrong). Wavy = Rossby waves. They steer storms, carry western disturbances (Mediterranean extra-tropical cyclones, dragged in by the subtropical westerly jet), control the South Asian monsoon, mix troposphere and stratosphere (ozone-depleting substances).
  • Climate change: Arctic warms faster → smaller temperature contrast → weaker, more meandering jets → long heatwaves, coldwaves, droughts or floods.
  • Heat dome: stagnant high pressure; sinking air compresses and warms; mid/high latitudes, continental climates. Polar vortex: cold air held by the polar jet; meanders let it spill south. DANA: isolated depression at high levels (cut-off low).
  • Stratospheric cooling: CO₂ in thin stratosphere radiates heat to space; ozone loss = less UV heating. Effects: slower ozone recovery, more PSCs, stronger polar vortex, disrupted jets. "Warm troposphere + cooling stratosphere" is the fingerprint of human-caused change (GHGs affected it by ~1885).

Local winds (name → hook)

Wind Where Hook
Chinook E. Rockies (USA, Canada) warm dry, "snow eater"
Foehn Alps (leeward) warm dry descending
Sirocco (Ghibli, Chili, Khamsin) Sahara → Mediterranean hot, dry; rainy in S. Europe
Harmattan W. Africa (Sahara → Guinea) dry, dusty NE trade; "Doctor" wind
Loo N. India, Pakistan, May–June furious, hot, heatstroke
Bora Adriatic (Italy, Slovenia, Croatia) extremely cold dry NE, katabatic
Mistral Rhône valley (France) cold NW
Santa Ana S. California hot dry; worsens wildfires
Khamsin Egypt dusty spring wind, up to 50 days
Purga Siberia, Russian steppes icy NE blizzard wind
Pamperos Pampas (Argentina, Uruguay, Brazil) violent cold SW

🧣 Hot vs cold: Chinook, Foehn, Sirocco, Harmattan, Loo, Santa Ana = hot/warm · Bora, Mistral, Purga, Pamperos = cold. Mistral & Bora = "Brrr" winds.

Monsoon (PYQ 2014, ans C): seasonal reversal of winds is typical of the monsoon climate.

3 · Moisture, clouds, precipitation, storms

  • Humidity: absolute (g/m³) · relative (% of what air can hold) · specific (g per kg). Dew point = saturation temperature. Dew forms when a surface falls below dew point; no dew on cloudy nights because clouds send the Earth's radiation back (PYQ 2019, ans B). Frost = deposition (vapour → ice). Fog = near-surface cloud. Smog = smoke + fog (sulphurous and photochemical). Haze = dry particles.
  • Atmospheric rivers: narrow moisture corridors (can carry more water than the Amazon) pushed by westerlies/jet streams to mid-latitudes → heavy rain, floods.

☁️ Clouds by height: High (>6,000 m) = Cirrus – wispy ice "chicken feathers" · Mid (2,000–6,000 m) = Alto- · Low (<2,000 m) = Stratus, stratocumulus, nimbostratus · Cumulonimbus = vertical tower (thunder, hail, tornado). Clouds & climate (PYQ 2022, ans D): high thin clouds trap heat; low thick clouds reflect – so both statements (high cool, low warm) are wrong. PYQ 2019 (ans D): cirrus thinning and sulphate aerosols in the stratosphere are geo-engineering to reduce global warming.

  • Polar stratospheric clouds: 15–25 km, polar winter, below −78 °C; "nacreous / mother-of-pearl"; surfaces for ozone destruction (Antarctic ozone hole).
  • Cloud seeding: silver iodide, potassium iodide, salt, dry ice → hygroscopic nuclei; by aircraft or ground generators; for rain, snowpack, fog clearing, hail suppression; works only if moisture exists.
Precipitation How Where
Convectional heated air rises → cumulonimbus; short, intense, thunder tropics 0–30°
Orographic air forced up mountains; rain shadow on lee side mountains
Frontal warm air over cooler (warm front = long steady; cold front = short intense) mid-latitudes 30–60°
Cyclonic convection/frontal on a large scale around a low cyclones

Thunderstorm: 3 stages – cumulus → mature → dissipating. Ice/water collisions give lighter + charge at the top, heavier − charge at the bottom → lightning (air excited N₂/O₂), thunder; lightning conductors on tall buildings. Tornado: rotating funnel from a thunderstorm; >300 km/h; Tornado Alley (Texas → Nebraska) where warm moist Gulf air meets cold dry Canadian air and warm dry desert air → supercells. Waterspouts: over water; fair-weather vs tornadic. Water vapour (PYQ 2024, ans a): amount decreases with altitude; it is not maximum at the poles.

4 · Air masses, fronts, cyclones

  • Air mass: big air body that took on the character of its source (high-pressure, calm regions). Types: mT, cT, mP, cP, cA (+ equatorial). Tropical = warm, polar = cold, continental = dry, maritime = moist. Examples: mT → Amazon, SE Asia rain; cT → Sahara, central Australia; mP → UK, Ireland, Japan Sea coast snow; cP → Siberia, Canadian prairies; cA → N. Canada, Scandinavia cold spells.
  • Fronts: boundary of two air masses; frontogenesis (formation) / frontolysis (death); mid-latitudes; bigger contrast = thinner front; cold fronts move faster.

⚔️ Cold front = Crash (cumulonimbus, thunder, hail) · Warm front = Wet blanket (stratus/cirrostratus, steady drizzle, fog) · Stationary = stalemate (light rain for days) · Occluded = cold overtakes warm (warm or cold occlusion).

Tropical vs temperate cyclones

Tropical Temperate (extra-tropical)
Origin Thermal Dynamic (frontal)
Latitude 10–30° 35–65° (more pronounced in N. Hemisphere – bigger temperature contrast)
Forms over warm seas only land and sea
Size 100–500 km 300–2,000 km
Rain heavy, but not beyond a few hours slow, for many days, even weeks
Wind 100–250 km/h; more damage from wind, surge, torrential rain 30–150 km/h; more damage from flooding
Life not more than a week 2–3 weeks
Fronts absent created by fronts
India both coasts hit, east coast hot-spot Western Disturbances

Names: Cyclone (Indian Ocean) · Hurricane (Atlantic) · Typhoon (W. Pacific, S. China Sea) · Willy-willy (W. Australia). Needs: sea-surface ≥ 26.5 °C (the PYQ note says >27 °C), moisture, low wind shear, a pre-existing disturbance, Coriolis. Depression ≤ 62 km/h → cyclone ≥ 64 knots (74 mph). Structure: eye (calm, clear), eyewall (worst winds/rain), rainbands. Impacts: wind, rain, storm surge, tornadoes. PYQ 2015 (ans B): no cyclones in the S. Atlantic / SE Pacific because the ITCZ seldom occurs there (also strong wind shear, cooler SST, no spin to start). PYQ 2020 (ans C): only some cyclones develop an eye; the eye is not 10 °C cooler. Climate change: warmer seas → more intense storms, more Cat 4–5 (Arabian Sea, N. Atlantic), fewer overall, poleward shift, slower movement, rapid intensification, sea-level rise worsens surge. Temperate cyclones also shift poleward and bring heavier rain.

5 · Climatic regions (Köppen)

🔤 Köppen letters: A–tropical humid · B–dry · C–warm temperate · D–cold snow-forest · E–polar · H–highland. Second letters: f no dry season · w winter dry · s dry summer · m monsoon. "All Big Cities Deserve Extra Halwa."

Climate (code) Where Look-for hooks (as printed)
Equatorial (Af) 10°N–S: Amazon, Congo, Indonesia, PNG 24–27 °C, tiny annual range; convectional 4 pm rain, no dry month; evergreen selvas, hardwoods (mahogany, rosewood, ebony), almost no undergrowth, leached soil; hunters-gatherers, slash-and-burn
Savannah (Aw) 10–30°, continental interiors: Sudan, Venezuela, Brazil, N. Australia hot rainy summer, dry winter; tall grass (elephant grass), baobab; Masai pastoralism; "Big Game country"
Tropical monsoon (Am) 10–30°, E. continental margins: India, Vietnam 3 seasons; 200–250 cm; teak, sal; intensive paddy
Hot desert (BWh) W. margins of tropical land, subtropical high, cold currents: Sahara, Kalahari, Mojave, Atacama xerophytes (waxy/thorny leaves, deep roots, succulent stems), date palms at oases; Bedouin, Tuareg, Bushmen
Cold desert (BWk) continental interiors: Gobi, Patagonia wide annual range, cold winters; bunchgrasses
Steppe (BS) 45–60°, mid-continental: Prairies, Steppes, Downs warm summers, cold winters; Chernozem; wheat/maize, ranching
Mediterranean (Cs) 30–45°, west margins: California, Chile, SW S. Africa, SW Australia hot dry summer, winter rain (westerlies); orchards (citrus, olives), vineyards; cork oak, eucalyptus
Marine West Coast (Cfb, "British type") 45–60°, west margins: NW Europe, SW S. America, NZ mild, rain all year, small annual range; temperate deciduous forest; dairy
China type (Cw / Cfa; Gulf & Natal types) 30–45°, east margins: SE China, Japan warm moist summer, cool dry winter; typhoons; most productive mid-latitude farming
Taiga / Siberian (Df) 50/60–70°: N. Canada, Eurasia −30 to −40 °C winters; evergreen conifers (softwood, pure stands); fur farms, lumbering
Manchurian / Laurentian (Dw) E. margins, N. Hemisphere only: Manchuria, Japan, NE America cold dry winters, wet warm summers; cool temperate forest
Polar (ET, EF) Greenland, N. Canada, Alaska, Antarctica summer < 10 °C; mosses, lichens; Eskimos, Lapps, Yakuts

Handout alert: the Köppen group table labels Df = humid continental and Dw = subarctic, but the regional table labels Taiga = Df and Manchurian = Dw. Remember the names and places, not the D-codes. Numbers in the regional table (e.g. "150–1000 cm" for Af) are printed as-is and look scrambled – don't memorise them.

Climate PYQs in one glance | Year | Asked | Answer / rule | |---|---|---| | 2011 | Rainforest regenerates slowly | Soil poor in nutrients (leached, nutrients stored in plants; rapid decay) | | 2011 | African–Eurasian desert belt | Subtropical high-pressure cells (not warm currents). Rain-shadow (Gobi) and cold currents (Namib, Atacama) are other causes | | 2012 | Tropical savannah | Definite dry and wet season | | 2015 | "Clear morning, heat builds, thunder, short rain" | Equatorial (ITCZ; two rainfall peaks) | | 2018 | Desert leaf modifications | Hard waxy, tiny, thorns – all three | | 2021 | What keeps savannah forest in check | Fire, grazing herbivores, seasonal rainfall (2, 3, 4) | | 2021 | Fast leaf-litter decay, bare soil, epiphytes | Tropical rain forest | | 2023 | Rainforest soil rich in nutrients? | Statement I wrong; II right (fast decay, nutrients absorbed) | | 2024 | Low annual/daily range, rain all year, 50–250 cm | Marine West Coast | | no year | Dust in subtropical/temperate areas | I correct (deserts, wind); II wrong – these have strong dry winds |

Recall sheet#

Traps: "Jet streams only in the Northern Hemisphere" ✘ · "Temperature contrast of land-sea is greater in summer" ✘ (winter) · "Westerlies 30°N–60°S" ✘ · "Ozone causes radio reflection" ✘ · "More moisture aloft makes it colder" ✘ · "Gulf Stream is a cold current" ✘ (statement 2 in PYQ 2024 is wrong) · "Eye is 10 °C cooler" ✘ · "Rainforest soil is rich" ✘.
